note: QTS's 18-building, 1,200 MW campus: about 700 acres rezoned in November 2025 and 914 more in April 2026. City leaders signed NDAs, and two council members who backed it lost their seats in August.

Regulators ruled half of the 6 million sq ft, 1.2 GW plan violates the Coastal Zone Act, citing 516 diesel generators, and an appeals board agreed. The rest still needs a county rezoning; the governor opposes it.
An air-permit hearing is set for Dec. 7; project bonds and tax breaks remain under challenge.

Project Cannoli: six buildings on 282 acres near Detroit Metro Airport. Site plan approved 5–1 on Oct. 14 with site work underway; Google expects to draw power by late 2027 under a 20-year DTE contract.

place: Maricopa County near Luke Air Force Base
note: Two data centers and a 700 MW gas plant on 160 acres near Luke Air Force Base. Supervisors approved the military-area permit 4–1; the air-quality permit was still pending.
A Pima County judge dismissed the rezoning challenge; TEP utility terms and public-record disputes continue. The repository identifies affiliates, not a single operating developer.

A 1,000-acre hyperscale campus and gas plant on the former Tailgate Ranch near Tonganoxie. More than 1,000 residents spoke against it; the county let its moratorium lapse and has not voted on the project.

place: Town of Turtle and Town of Beloit
note: Both towns rejected Panattoni's cost-reimbursement agreement for the $1 billion, 2 million sq ft campus in July 2026 and began 12-month moratoriums.
Forsyth commissioners denied the rezoning 5–2 after the planning board recommended against it; the three-building campus would have sat across from Rural Hall's town hall.

Administrative approval expanded the approved building area from roughly 240,000 to about 700,000 square feet. County officials also rejected the underlying AI campus 5–1 before the later administrative action.
Planners approved the project with a 50 MW cap; the council postponed appeals to April 13, 2027, over noise and utility-rate questions.

County Executive Jessica Fitzwater rejected the campus's development agreement and extended the county's pause on new applications to July 2027. It had been Maryland's only approved hyperscale project.
A developer withdrew the Matthews proposal after local review and opposition. The repository does not establish the owner or reported power/acreage.
Planning approval covers phase one of the 300-acre hyperscale campus; construction is expected to begin in 2027.
The 1.7-million-square-foot air-cooled campus received final county approval. Construction is expected in early 2027; the county estimates nearly $10 million in annual property tax.
Construction was halted by a temporary restraining order while environmental litigation proceeds; the roughly 500-acre campus also awaits state air, stormwater and transmission reviews.
Montgomery County approved up to $100 billion in industrial revenue bonds and a 25-year Chapter 100 agreement for Google's reported $15 billion campus.
The county sold land and approved 20-year property tax breaks before publicly identifying Amazon as the developer of the $10 billion campus.
The Army conditionally selected CyrusOne for exclusive talks on a 1,201-acre federal lease, with a fiscal 2029 target and the developer to supply its own power and water.
Coweta rezoned 320 acres 3–2 in 2025 for the reported $1 billion project. The county's later moratoriums cover new applications, not this approval.
Regulators approved dedicated gas plants for the expansion; about 5.3 GW of supply is in the filing set.
The six-building, three-substation application was withdrawn hours before Fauquier planners were to review it, the third Remington-area data center application pulled in a month.
County supervisors unanimously denied the plan amendment for the 43-million-square-foot, 2,000-acre proposal.
Courts voided the 2,100-acre, 37-building rezoning over flawed hearing notices, an appeals court agreed in March, and QTS terminated the project July 2, 2026.
A 14-building, 578-acre Archbald 1 LLC proposal was denied unanimously after nine hearings; an appeal is expected.
Coweta rezoned 829 acres 3–2 in April 2026 for nine buildings totaling 4.34 million sq ft, with 17 conditions, after a moratorium and a new county ordinance.
A construction permit for the 300,000 sq ft first phase on Lower Moncure Road was issued Sept. 25; PointOne puts phase one at about $900 million.
The roughly 1,000-acre Sanford Woods proposal along the Mousam River is blocked by a local pause; the developer remains unreported.
A 50–100 MW campus discussed for Summit View Business Park, uncovered through public records requests; a supervisor said in August it would not proceed.
Approved 3–2 with a 20-year, $1.15 billion tax break for a campus with a 1,000 MW base capacity. The end user is unnamed, and neighbors have sued; construction is expected to start next year.
The 500 MW, $19.4 billion campus near STAMP is under review while a tribal and environmental-law suit challenges the zoning agreement.
TVA approved up to 300 MW for xAI's Memphis operations, including the Colossus sites and related expansion.
Runs on gas turbines at a former power plant. The state permitted 41 permanent turbines and set a retirement schedule for temporary ones; a judge let the NAACP's Clean Air Act suit proceed.
A judge ruled the 750 MW project can proceed despite Chatham County's moratorium, which otherwise stays in force; damages are still to be decided.
A $1.8 billion AI campus under construction on the former Merck site; more than 100 residents protested at a June council meeting, and the mayor defends it as replacing lost tax revenue.
Oracle is challenging Wisconsin's credit and collateral rules for the Port Washington campus it shares with OpenAI and Vantage; transmission review remains unresolved.
Ranalli filed a 300 MW grid request but no town application; the site was listed for sale. Lysander's pause and the state's 50 MW permitting freeze both cover it.
Exempt from Birmingham's six-month pause on data centers over 20 MW. Alabama Power filed its power contract with key terms blacked out.
Phase one is 150 MW with a possible 1 GW at full build. The Quorum Court rejected a moratorium with an AVAIO carve-out in July, then passed rules in September with no carve-out.
Entergy charges customers through a rider for the Cypress Solar project serving the campus. A judge rejected Entergy's bid to keep its Google agreements out of the press.
Residents sought a moratorium on the proposed project. The board adopted zoning rules instead and twice rejected a pause on 4–4 ties.
Courts upheld the town clerk's rejection of referendum petitions against the January 2026 rezoning, so no public vote is scheduled. Gov. Hobbs vetoed a related petition bill.
A five-building campus on land already zoned for it, which exempts it from Phoenix's newer data center rules. Neighbors brought complaints to the attorney general's town hall in October.
Would have been Arizona's largest data center, even after being cut from 59 buildings to 11. Supervisors denied the rezoning 4–1 over water, power, noise and wildlife concerns.
The council voted 5–2 to sell 500 acres of city land with a feasibility period; no data center is approved. A referendum petition was disqualified on technical grounds.
The council voted unanimously against the project in December 2025 after residents raised noise and water concerns.
QTS asked to add 98 diesel backup generators to the 40 already installed. State air regulators were still reviewing the request in mid-2026.
Commissioners approved a $19.3 million property tax rebate over 35 years for a facility expected to create 16 jobs. Every public commenter opposed it.
Approved 5–0 on the former Carestream site. The first phase is 27.5 MW, with long-term plans of up to 1 GW.
The developer withdrew a 2.5 million sq ft rezoning application in October 2026, a day before the council's first vote on a moratorium.
Neighbors' protests prompted a proposed indefinite moratorium, which would not apply to this pending application.
A 2023 host agreement worth $231 million survived a 2025 vote, with building permits due by March 2026. A project database now lists the deal as terminated.
Commissioners raised noise, height and airport concerns in June 2025; a year later it still had no approval.
Rezoned in 2025 with a $150 million tax break, then approved in April 2026 under a 20-year deal. Residents sued and started recall petitions, and the campus still needs a regional water permit.
Applications were withdrawn in June 2026 after the planning commission rejected the land-use change.
Seven buildings proposed on about 113 acres. The city's 18-month moratorium lets review continue but bars final approval while it is in effect.
Withdrawn the day before the sole commissioner was to rule, after planners voted 6–1 to recommend denial.
Commissioners unanimously rejected it after hundreds of residents turned out against it.
AWS bought 985 acres for $270 million; the county then paused new data centers.
Commissioners rejected it 4–1 even after it was scaled down from 11 buildings.
Under construction off Gordon Highway near Haynes Station and exempt from both the city's pause, extended 60 days in July, and the ordinance passed 6–5 in October.

OpenAI's $20 billion campus near Rincon would draw 3.2 GW from Georgia Power. The deal was negotiated in secret and announced in July, prompting protests and nearby moratoriums in Savannah and Chatham County.
A 15-building campus planned across from two schools. The developer withdrew in August and is pursuing housing instead; the city then banned data centers.
Residents sued, saying the county broke its own rules approving the rezoning.
The council cleared a temporary occupancy permit for the first building near the airport in June 2026; one member suggested pausing further projects until it proves its water and energy claims.
Alliant has confidential rate agreements with QTS and proposes three gas peaker plants, which a business group asked regulators to scrutinize.
A proposed 1,100-acre campus cited by a regional business paper urging developers to disclose water, power and tax terms.
Karis eyed farmland east of the airport. The county adopted a 12-month moratorium, and the city ordered up a six-month pause after 76% of survey respondents opposed large data centers.
Salix annexed 900 acres for a possible site, which Woodbury County's 12-month moratorium does not cover.
An initial agreement signed in December prompted residents to push for the 90-day moratorium adopted in September.
Rezoned 3–2. A judge rejected farmers' challenge in May 2026, and they appealed to the Idaho Supreme Court.
A hearing examiner denied the permit and the council upheld it 4–1. The developer asked for reconsideration.
Seeks federal land near Boise for a campus with its own gas plant. BLM expects to begin formal review by year-end; Boise's mayor opposes it.
Annexation approved 8–1 in March 2026. Residents sued to void it, and Joliet Township votes Nov. 3 on an advisory question about approving AI data centers.
The county's moratorium was ruled invalid, but Latham canceled its annexation vote and the county tabled flawed applications. Hut 8 could resubmit.
The county board approved a conditional use 17–10 in April 2026. Neighbors sued to overturn it; a hearing was postponed.
A liquid-cooled facility approved by right in 2024 and unaffected by the city's 180-day pause.
Annexed and zoned in 2025. More than 120 residents packed a July 2026 council meeting to oppose it.
Has a building permit. Residents sued in July 2026, arguing data centers aren't a permitted use and that closed-door talks broke open-meetings law.
An existing annexation agreement already allows data centers here, so Rockford's six-month moratorium does not cover it.
The village board unanimously rejected annexation in August 2026, then adopted a one-year moratorium.
A review committee has met repeatedly since August 2026 on the planned unit development. No zoning hearing is scheduled.
Nearly finished, and exempt from Jeffersonville's one-year moratorium.
Cited by building trades as a model for its school-tax agreement.
Cited by building trades for Amazon's infrastructure funding agreement.
Granted about $85 million in tax abatements at the same meeting that ratified the city's moratorium. Expected to create 75 jobs.

Google's $2 billion campus has operated since December with more buildings planned. In October the council rejected a moratorium and study commission prompted by neighbors' noise and light complaints.
A proposed moratorium that could run to July 2028 would exempt it, drawing objections from residents and the pause's original sponsors.
Regulators approved AES Indiana's $737 million plan to power it. Google pays $32.3 million directly; $73.8 million in upgrades goes into rates.
Regulators approved NIPSCO's special contract with Amazon; the utility says data centers fund the power serving them.
Annexed quickly and backed 6–1 by planners despite heavy opposition and questions about who owns it. Emporia votes Nov. 3 on a citizen ban that would block it.
The city ended its land sale contract in September 2026. Voters decide a 25 MW data center ban Nov. 3.
Grew in size while planned water use fell and the tax abatement and city power commitment were dropped. No application has been filed.
The developer scrapped it after the county's moratorium.
Rejected unanimously in October 2025; the county then adopted a 12-month moratorium.
Three 200,000 sq ft buildings with on-site gas power. Rejected in 2025, then approved by planners in March 2026; residents sued, and TenKey is suing the county over its permit rules.
The city paused data centers for a year, and the developer sued.
About 2,080 acres were rezoned in May 2026 before Meta was revealed as the user. A think tank estimates about $50 million a year in tax breaks.
A hyperscale project planned at an idled aluminum mill prompted neighboring Daviess County to adopt a moratorium.
The EastPark campus is exempt from both counties' six-month moratoriums; TeraWulf expects the first 500 MW to ramp in late 2028.
Opposition to the plan helped drive the city's six-month pause on new data center applications.
The county unanimously rejected rules that would have allowed hyperscale siting next to a coal plant; Burgin is weighing annexation instead.
Would have been New England's largest. The planning board denied a permit extension in October 2026, letting the 2021 permit lapse; Servistar never bought the land.
The state approved 172 diesel backup generators after a 2024 law exempted backup generators from power plant certification.
Covered by the county's 18-month moratorium; the developer had appealed the earlier executive order.
Amazon withdrew in August 2026 after voter backlash in the June primary, and the county paused site plans.
The select board halted talks in November 2025 after residents organized; little was disclosed about the end user or power source.
Would fill an existing warehouse at the former Loring base using immersion cooling.
Voted down in December 2025 after swift opposition.
Gov. Mills cited this locally backed project when she vetoed a statewide pause in April 2026.
A one-year moratorium covers the former steel plant site.
The local utility halted water and sewer service to new data centers for a year, and the township paused large utility structures for six months.
Voters overturned the rezoning, about 90% no.
Broke ground in June 2026. The attorney general is asking an appeals court to void DTE's heavily redacted power contracts, and the lieutenant governor now opposes it.
The city exempted it from its moratorium in September 2026 to end the developer's lawsuit.

developer: Elk River Capital and Swervo Development
note: The council refused the zoning change in July 2026, then adopted a one-year moratorium.
Google dropped its 28-year tax abatement request and offered a $210 million decommissioning guarantee. The council votes on the permit Oct. 26.
Approved 4–1 in 2024. Neighbors dropped their lawsuit in September 2026 after running out of money, clearing the way for construction.
Planners recommended the rezoning and permit 4–1 in October 2026; the council has the final vote.
The city denied an interim use permit after finding unpermitted chillers, and the developer sued over Minnesota's first data center moratorium.
Residents' open-meetings suit says officials hid water, power and abatement terms; a judge weighed dismissal.
Approved in March 2026 and exempt from the city's 180-day pause.
A pending application exempt from the city's 180-day pause.
Two 20,000 sq ft buildings blocked by the county's six-month moratorium. The developer sued, and a judge kept a restraining order in place.
Rezoned in September 2026 against the zoning commission's advice. Residents promised lawsuits.
Rezoned in September 2026 near the Shaw Nature Reserve, with new county noise and setback rules.
The plan commission rejected the 384-foot tower 6–0 after 475 opposition letters.
Certified for state tax exemptions plus a $4 million site grant. Mississippi Power will supply about 500 MW.
Approved for state tax exemptions, with county and city infrastructure incentives.
Rezoned to light industrial with conditions including a $5 million impact fee and 1,000-foot buffers; no developer is named, and residents have challenged the rezoning in court.
Covered by the city's July 2026 pause on data center approvals.
Sabey ended the deal in May 2026 after another company used a purchase right on much of the site.
County commissioners say state law keeps them from regulating it and asked lawmakers for more authority.
Dropped in August 2025 after backlash over water and power use.
Rejected 6–1 in 2025. The developer sued, then settled and said it would not build there.
Rezoned 8–0 in 2025 and exempt from the city's 2026 pause.
Withdrawn in March 2026 during the town's zoning debate; Apex then adopted a moratorium.
Plans filed after the county rezoned land along U.S. 158. It's the state's largest active proposal.
Rezoned 3–2 on Sept. 14 after the January approval was voided over a defective hearing notice; the planning board had recommended denial.
Site plan approved for two 125,000 sq ft colocation buildings, with water capped at 75,000 gallons a month and no city tax incentives.
Regulators approved a roughly $110 million power project for the campus near Harwood, described as nearing completion.
Energized another 75 MW in July 2026. Aberdeen, South Dakota, has trucked over a million gallons of water to it.
A gas-powered campus near schools; the developer plans to apply once city rules are final.
The developer offered $140 million in benefits and a home value guarantee to head off a proposed 24-month moratorium.
Permit approved 5–0 in September 2026, replacing a 100 MW bitcoin mine. First phase due late 2027.
The village board granted zoning in October 2026; no construction timeline yet.
Eversource is studying service for a possible hyperscale project at the closed coal plant. No application has been filed; the governor opposes it.
Blocked by the township's ban; the developer is suing for over $300 million in federal court.
The planning board is weighing a revised self-powered plan; residents raised LNG storage, emissions and noise concerns.
Withdrawn after the township banned data centers while it was pending.
Approved with a 1,265 MW solar facility to power it; the county offered no incentives.
Announced in November 2025; the county since adopted rules requiring closed-loop cooling.
Months of opposition led to a one-year county moratorium in June 2026.
The feasibility agreement ended in August 2026.
Protests over the solar-powered proposal led to an 18-month county moratorium.
Planners required a full environmental impact statement in July; the town's August pause exempts it as an earlier application.
Brookhaven's 18-month moratorium was aimed in part at this proposal.
The council rejected it in August 2026 and the developer went to court. Voters decide a 25 MW ban Nov. 3.
Two data centers and an 800 MW gas plant approved by emergency resolution. The Ohio Supreme Court revived a referendum, set for Nov. 3.
Applied before the village's 12-month moratorium and heads to a zoning appeals hearing.
Under construction, with a second campus proposed. Voters decide a 25 MW cap Nov. 3; the city says the first proceeds on existing permits.
s: News From The States (Ohio Capital Journal)

note: Residents petitioned for a special election to void the city's power agreement, and voters decide a data center ban Nov. 3.

note: Amazon is evaluating the site, which could draw about 30 times the county's power use. Township zoning initiatives are on the Nov. 3 ballot.
The Ohio Supreme Court let the village reject four data centers filed weeks before its ban.
The borough unanimously denied the 18-building application in March 2026.
Rejected unanimously at the historic state school site in May 2026; the developer appealed in June.
A 15-building complex on a former coal plateau, held up by a 180-day pause.
Under construction; it prompted the township's moratorium and new ordinance, which do not apply to it.
Nadara holds a purchase option from the Fay-Penn Economic Council but hasn't applied; the township adopted conditional-use rules in September.
The town banned data centers a day after the filing; the developer is appealing.
Seeks to expand on-site gas power from about 50 MW to 450 MW. Regulators ruled it isn't subject to power plant rules; it's exempt from the county's new freeze.
The first building has topped out. The campus is exempt from the county's 2026 pause.
A lawsuit settlement now bans data centers in most of the ACE Basin.
Cancelled because the developer could not secure enough power.
Its scale prompted the city council to form a committee to draft data center rules, due in January.
The gas-and-diesel-powered proposal prompted an 18-month city moratorium.
Planners approved the permit in a short April hearing. Residents appealed over notice; commissioners were unsure they could cancel it.

A state authority approved a 40,000-acre project area, later halved, overriding county zoning. Lawsuits, a referendum fight and water-right protests continue; the backlash cost several officials their primaries.
Planners approved up to five buildings with an on-site 1.5 GW gas plant after months of opposition.
Commissioners rejected residents' appeals of the data center and its gas, solar and water permits.
The council denied the overlay 7–0 despite a planning commission recommendation; the developer may reapply.
Paired 84 data centers with a 3,500 MW gas plant. Rejected 6–1, and the board refused to let it withdraw, blocking a refile for a year.
Planners recommended denial in 2025; the plan was withdrawn twice, most recently in August 2026.
Rejected 4–3; it projected up to 2 million gallons of water a day at peak.
Amazon's second Louisa campus, planned for 10 buildings and three substations; a neighbor's nuisance suit over brown water, dust and noise is proceeding in federal court.
Faces a proposed record $2.5 million state penalty after running 62 diesel generators for a week during a substation failure.
State regulators cited the site for seven runoff violations affecting streams and wetlands.
Deferred indefinitely after planners unanimously recommended denial.
Approved 4–3 in October 2026 with water-use limits and about $6.4 million in developer contributions.
The village approved 15 more data centers on two campuses on former Foxconn land in January 2026.
The 1,500-acre annexation bid was rejected, spurring neighboring towns to cap data center size.
Regulators approved its 220 MW Alliant contract with conditions; the chair criticized the deal's secrecy.
The council let the letter of intent lapse in June 2026 and later paused data centers; voters decide Nov. 3 on requiring a vote for big deals on the site.
Microsoft bought the land in early 2025 but has released no plan; residents want a moratorium or referendum.
The council denied the permit 7–0 after the developer missed deadlines to complete its application.
The first data center certified under the 2025 law that strips local zoning control; planners approved a concept plan in 2025.
An off-grid gas plant permitted as a minor source, with parts of the application kept confidential. Residents lost appeals; the state promised a citizen advisory council.
Air permits approved for off-grid gas plants to power data centers; a federal court dismissed residents' suit.
Site plans approved unanimously for a 1.8 GW first phase and a gas plant of up to 2.7 GW. Later phases need new review.
Permits approved for the campus and its off-grid power plant, with annual water-use reporting. A residents' challenge was dismissed.
Commissioners are drafting conditions and weighing an exemption that would bypass the state siting council.
A planned 16-building campus on land bought from the Port of Walla Walla under an NDA. Amazon filed its site application in August; residents want a moratorium and an environmental impact statement.
Blocked when Nye County banned data centers in the over-appropriated Pahrump groundwater basin; the developer had projected about 300 acre-feet of water use a year.
The developer's $100 million federal suit led Hill County to rescind its moratorium and adopt a disclosure checklist instead.
A $5.1 billion campus with a 600,000 sq ft first phase. Gov. Kotek pulled the state land sale in July, and Salem's 120-day moratorium bars construction through at least Jan. 19.
A judge set aside the county's approvals and required a full environmental impact report; developer Sebastian Rucci plans to seek a new trial or appeal and is weighing other sites.
The first data center approved on federal public land, by amending a solar permit. An appeals board halted it in September and let BLM redo its review in October.

n: South Valley and Peru Ridge campuses
note: Regulators approved two temporary gas plants to power the campuses until NV Energy can serve them; air and county permits are still needed. South Valley received $23.35 million in tax abatements and is reportedly leased to Nvidia.

place: North Slope, near the Dalton Highway
note: The state issued a preliminary finding backing a 50-year land lease. Power would come from North Slope gas through a new pipeline; a gas supply and federal wetlands permit are not yet secured.
Its air permit was under review when Gov. Kotek ordered regulators to stop issuing data center permits until July 2027; residents had petitioned for a hearing.
The city manager says Amazon canceled several planned campuses after the state permit pause, which he estimates costs the city about $550 million in future fees.
Stuck at the pre-application stage after Gilroy extended its moratorium; Amazon's first Gilroy campus is under construction.
The council upheld staff approval 8–0, rejecting a labor-led appeal, as San Jose writes standards for 20 MW-plus projects instead of pausing.
Opposition to this proposal fueled Monterey Park's voter-approved ban; the developer withdrew.
